This game could be so much better then it actually is. I am not sure how they manage to keep the price sky high because it is ultimately not that great.  Some of it is kinda great, but then it just pilllars out down into arcade slush.

If you can get it for less then 7$USD it is worth it.

EARTH DEFENSE FORCE 5 is an unapologetically excessive third-person shooter that turns a global alien invasion into a celebration of gigantic enemies, overwhelming firepower, collapsing cities, and wonderfully chaotic battles. Developed by SANDLOT and published by D3PUBLISHER, it does not attempt to compete with realistic military shooters in visual sophistication or cinematic presentation. Instead, it builds its identity around enormous battles and a deliberately theatrical science-fiction atmosphere. The result is rough around the edges but consistently entertaining for players who appreciate action games that prioritize spectacle and replayability.

The campaign follows humanity's struggle against an extraterrestrial force known as the Primers. What begins as an alarming attack quickly develops into a worldwide catastrophe involving giant insects, flying creatures, enormous monsters, advanced spacecraft, and heavily armed humanoid aliens. The narrative is presented with complete seriousness despite increasingly ridiculous circumstances. Soldiers shout desperate reports, commanders issue dramatic orders, and humanity repeatedly appears to be approaching extinction. This contrast between earnest military dialogue and outrageous events creates much of the game's personality. The story itself is straightforward, but it effectively provides context for an escalating sequence of enormous battles.

Its combat is built around quantity as much as individual enemy design. Instead of confronting a handful of carefully positioned opponents, players can find themselves facing entire streets filled with giant ants, skies crowded with airborne creatures, or squads of towering extraterrestrial soldiers firing from several directions. Encounters can become wonderfully messy as explosions fill the screen, buildings collapse, enemies swarm friendly troops, and radio conversations continue amid the destruction. Enemy artificial intelligence is relatively simple, but the sheer numbers and variety of threats compensate by forcing constant movement and prioritization.

The four playable classes provide significantly different experiences. Ranger offers traditional infantry combat with familiar weapons and straightforward mobility, making it the easiest starting point. Wing Diver sacrifices conventional durability for exceptional aerial mobility and energy weapons, allowing players to fly over enemies and rapidly reposition themselves. Air Raider specializes in support equipment and powerful attacks that can dramatically influence large engagements. Fencer is a heavily equipped combat specialist capable of carrying formidable weapon combinations, although mastering its movement and equipment requires more practice. Switching between these classes can make familiar missions feel substantially different.

Weapon collection is one of the strongest reasons to continue playing. Battles reward equipment that gradually expands the available arsenal, and higher difficulty settings encourage players to pursue increasingly powerful gear. The constant possibility of discovering a useful weapon creates a satisfying progression loop. Loadout experimentation also matters because certain weapons perform exceptionally well against particular enemy formations while proving inefficient in other circumstances. Choosing the right equipment can therefore transform a difficult mission from an exhausting struggle into a manageable engagement.

The campaign contains a tremendous number of missions, giving players a substantial amount of content even before considering repeated runs on different difficulties. Some scenarios inevitably become repetitive, particularly when familiar environments and enemy types return. However, the game frequently compensates by increasing the scale or introducing new combinations of threats. The enormous mission count also suits its progression system because replaying previous operations with different classes, equipment, or cooperative partners remains worthwhile.

Cooperative play greatly enhances the experience. Online missions allow four players to combine the strengths of different classes, creating opportunities for coordinated attacks, rescues, defensive positions, and spectacularly destructive strategies. Local split-screen is another welcome feature. Cooperation makes the battlefield chaos even more enjoyable because players can specialize rather than attempting to handle every threat individually. Reviving a fallen teammate while surrounded by enormous insects or coordinating attacks against gigantic enemies produces exactly the sort of memorable situations the game handles best.

Presentation is considerably less polished than the gameplay ambitions might suggest. Character models, textures, animations, environmental details, and certain effects can appear dated, while performance may struggle when battles become exceptionally crowded. Yet graphical fidelity is not the primary attraction. The game is impressive because of what it attempts to display simultaneously. Large groups of enemies can dominate streets and skies while explosions and environmental destruction transform previously recognizable urban areas into chaotic battlefields. There is an appealing sense that the developers willingly sacrificed refinement in favor of scale.

The sound design supports this atmosphere with constant gunfire, explosions, creature noises, military communications, and enthusiastic voice acting. Dialogue frequently becomes melodramatic, but that is an essential component of the experience rather than an accidental weakness. Soldiers continue shouting heroic declarations while humanity faces increasingly absurd disasters, giving the campaign the character of an interactive science-fiction monster movie.

Steam Deck compatibility is classified as Playable and is less straightforward than on a conventional Windows gaming PC. The game does not have an ideal officially optimized handheld experience, so players should expect possible compatibility or performance considerations when running it on Steam Deck. Its controller-focused third-person gameplay is naturally suitable for handheld controls, but enormous battles can place substantial demands on hardware. Players primarily purchasing it for Steam Deck should therefore approach it as a title that may require adjustments rather than expecting completely seamless performance in every mission.

Its greatest weaknesses are repetition, dated technology, uneven performance, simplistic enemy behavior, and a campaign structure that can become tiring during long sessions. Players seeking polished cinematic storytelling or cutting-edge graphics may struggle to understand its appeal. For the right audience, however, these shortcomings are outweighed by the enormous arsenal, varied classes, rewarding equipment progression, cooperative gameplay, huge campaign, and extraordinary battlefield scale.

Ultimately, EARTH DEFENSE FORCE 5 succeeds through commitment to its own ridiculous concept. Few shooters are willing to place hundreds of oversized enemies between the player and victory while simultaneously providing enough destructive equipment to make surviving such situations plausible. It is technically imperfect but mechanically generous, endlessly enthusiastic, and particularly enjoyable with friends. Beneath its dated exterior is an exceptionally entertaining action game that understands that sometimes saving Earth should involve gigantic insects, impossible odds, deafening explosions, and an unreasonable amount of firepower.

Rating: 9/10
